metaDescription: Six compact corded immersion blenders from 300W to 400W compared on speed control, shaft length, attachments, duty cycle and pan protection.
expertTake: The Cuisinart CSB-179 is the best small immersion blender, because its quiet DC motor, variable speed and 8 inch shaft behave well in small pots. The KitchenAid KHBV53 is the pick if you protect nonstick pans. The Turelar 400W is the value pick. If you blend ice, frozen fruit or large batches, skip small stick blenders and buy a countertop blender.
introParagraphs: An immersion blender is a motor in a handle with a short shaft and a blade at the end. You put the blade in the food instead of pouring food into a jar, which makes it the right tool for soup in the pot, sauces, dressings and small smoothies. Small models save drawer space, but their wattage and duty cycle set firm limits.

This guide explains how to judge motor power, speed control, shaft length and attachments on compact stick blenders, and what each can and cannot do. Start with the picks above for the short list, then read the reviews below to match a blender to your kitchen, your pots and the kind of cooking you actually do.

products.name: Cuisinart CSB-179 Smart Stick 300W Variable Speed Hand Blender

specList.label: Switch
specList.value: Push button for continuous or pulse

specList.label: Attachments
specList.value: 3 cup chopper and grinder, chef's whisk

specList.label: Guard
specList.value: Blade guard bell to cut splatter

products.description:
The Cuisinart CSB-179 is the small immersion blender that does the most with a 300 watt motor. A DC motor is smoother and quieter than the cheap universal motors in many budget blenders, and a continuous variable speed control lets you start slow and ramp up, which is the trick that prevents hot soup from spraying across the kitchen. An 8 inch stainless steel shaft reaches deep into a small pot or a quart jar.

The accessory set is what makes it a prep station. A 3 cup chopper and grinder handles herbs, nuts and breadcrumbs, a chef's whisk handles eggs and cream, and a 2 cup measuring cup suits dressings and small batches. A blade guard bell reduces splatter and keeps the blade from pulling toward the pot bottom. Compared with the KitchenAid KHBV53, it gives you a smaller jar but a whisk and chopper, and compared with the 400W budget models, it is lower in rated watts but better behaved at low speed.

Because the watts are modest, treat it as a tool for soup, sauces, smoothies and baby food rather than frozen fruit or ice. Start with the blade fully submerged, tilt slightly, and sweep up as the mix comes together. Unplug and press the release to detach the shaft, then wash the shaft, cup and chopper bowl, and wipe the motor body with a damp cloth. It is a good long-term pick for a small kitchen.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens that want variable speed, a chopper and a whisk from one compact stick.
pros: Quiet DC motor with continuous variable speed control
8 in shaft reaches deep into small pots and tall jars
Includes a chopper, whisk and measuring cup for extra jobs
Blade guard bell cuts splatter and protects cookware
cons: The 300W motor is not meant for ice or frozen fruit
Rated watts are lower than the 400W budget blenders
Extra attachments take up drawer space in a small kitchen

products.name: KitchenAid KHBV53 Variable Speed Corded Hand Blender

specList.label: Blending arm
specList.value: Removable 8 in with 4 point stainless blade

specList.label: Includes
specList.value: Hand blender, arm, jar, pan guard

products.description:
The KitchenAid KHBV53 is the small immersion blender for people who care about their cookware. A removable pan guard shields nonstick and enamel pots from the spinning blade, which is the most common way an immersion blender damages a pan. A 4 point stainless steel blade sits at the end of a removable 8 inch arm, and a trigger switch gives variable speed in one hand.

A 3 cup blending jar with a lid is included, and it doubles as a serving or storage container for a small batch such as a vinaigrette or hummus. Against the Cuisinart, you do not get a whisk or chopper, but you do get the pan guard and a bigger jar. Compared with the 300W and 400W budget machines, the trigger makes speed control easier, though the listing does not state a wattage.

Using it is straightforward. Press the trigger lightly to ramp speed and keep the blade below the surface to avoid splashes. The arm detaches and can go in the dishwasher, while the motor body should only be wiped. It suits someone who wants a better-built tool for occasional soup and smoothie jobs.
products.bestFor: Cooks with nonstick or enameled pots who want a pan guard and a trigger speed control.
pros: Removable pan guard protects nonstick and enamel cookware
Variable speed trigger gives one-handed speed control
The included 3 cup jar with a lid doubles as food storage
Arm detaches and is dishwasher safe for easy cleaning
cons: Wattage is not stated anywhere in the product listing, so power is hard to compare
No whisk or chopper attachment comes in the box with it
Costs more than the basic 300W and 400W sticks here

products.name: MasterChef 400W Immersion Blender with Variable Speed and Turbo
products.description:
The MasterChef is a 400 watt immersion blender with variable speed control and a turbo boost, a combination that gives it more punch than the 300 watt sticks while staying small. Variable speed lets you start gently for soup and push up for smoothies, and the turbo button adds a burst for tougher ingredients. The blending leg is stainless steel and detaches for cleaning.

It is a good match for soups, purees, baby food and emulsions. Compared with the Cuisinart, it has 100 more watts but no whisk or chopper, and compared with the 400W Turelar it adds variable speed rather than only two speeds. The listing says it is a licensed product of the television show, which signals a mass-market brand rather than an appliance specialist.

Treat the 400 watt number as a rough guide, since power also depends on the blade and shaft design. The motor body should never go in water, so wipe it with a damp cloth. Avoid long continuous runs and give the motor a rest between batches. It is a sensible small blender if you want variable speed without a premium price.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want variable speed and a turbo button at a modest price.
pros: 400W motor with variable speed and a turbo boost button
Detachable stainless steel leg is dishwasher safe for cleaning
Variable control suits both hot soup and cold smoothies
Compact enough to fit in a small kitchen drawer easily
cons: No whisk, chopper or jar is listed in the box contents
Brand is a licensed name, so support quality may vary
Motor body must be wiped clean and never washed in water

products.name: Turelar 400W Corded Immersion Blender with 2 Speeds

specList.label: Cleaning
specList.value: Detachable shaft, motor wiped with a damp cloth

products.description:
The Turelar is a simple 400 watt stick with a copper motor and two speeds plus a turbo setting. A pulse-activated control lets you blend in bursts, and the slim stainless shaft fits most bowls, pots and tall beakers. The two-pronged blade is said to avoid trapping stem fibers or leaves, which is a real annoyance with four-blade designs when you blend herbs or greens.

Compared with the OVENTE at 300 watts, it has 100 more watts and a turbo option for the same two-speed format. Against the MasterChef, it lacks continuous variable speed, so control is coarser. It is a good choice for a small batch of soup, a smoothie or baby food, and its detachable shaft makes cleaning easy. A top hanging ring lets you store it on a hook, which helps in a small kitchen.

Remember that the motor body should be wiped and not immersed. Do not blend very hard, frozen or fibrous items without cutting them small, and avoid long runs. If you want more control than two speeds, step up to the Cuisinart or MasterChef.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a basic, low cost 400W stick with a turbo setting.
pros: 400W copper motor gives more headroom than 300W models
Two-pronged blade resists trapping stems and leaves
Hanging ring makes storage easy in a small kitchen
Detachable shaft is simple to rinse clean after each use
cons: Only two speeds plus a turbo, so speed control is coarse
No jar, whisk or chopper is included in the box at all
Motor body is not immersible and must be wiped clean

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 3-in-1 Immersion Blender with Whisk and 24 oz Beaker

specList.label: Handle
specList.value: Soft grip, one handed speed control

specList.label: Duty cycle
specList.value: Under 1 minute per run, 30 minute rest after 5 cycles

products.description:
The Bonsenkitchen 3-in-1 is a starter kit that includes the blender, an egg whisk and a 24 ounce beaker. That is the combination most new owners actually use: blend soup in a pot, whisk eggs or cream and mix a dressing or smoothie in a beaker. One-handed speed control and a soft grip make it comfortable for small jobs.

The listing is unusually frank about duty cycle. It says each run should be under 1 minute, with a 30 minute rest after 5 consecutive cycles of one minute on and one minute off. That is a short duty cycle, and it tells you this is a light-use tool. Compared with the Turelar, it gives you a whisk and beaker but no stated wattage, and compared with the Cuisinart it lacks a quiet DC motor and variable control.

Treat it as a kitchen helper for occasional jobs. Remove stones from fruit, cut large items small and avoid frozen items. The detachable design allows the blades to be washed in the dishwasher, while the motor body should be wiped. If you blend daily, buy a stronger machine.
products.bestFor: First-time buyers who want a blender, whisk and beaker in one inexpensive set.
pros: Egg whisk and a 24 oz beaker are included in the kit
One handed speed control and a comfortable soft grip handle
Honest duty cycle guidance is given right in the listing
Detachable design lets the blades be washed very easily
cons: Short duty cycle limits it to under a minute per run
Wattage is not stated anywhere in the product listing
Only two speeds and no turbo or variable speed control

products.name: OVENTE HS560B 300W Corded Hand Blender with 2 Speeds
products.description:
The OVENTE HS560B is the plainest and lowest-cost option in this comparison. A 300 watt motor drives a slim stainless steel shaft through two speeds, with a pulse-activated sensor for short bursts. That is enough for sauces, dips, purees and a smoothie of soft ingredients, and it suits someone who blends once or twice a week.

The shaft detaches and is dishwasher safe, and a non-slip handle keeps it controllable. A 1 year limited warranty with US-based support is stated in the listing. Compared with the Turelar, it has 100 fewer watts and no turbo, and compared with the Cuisinart it lacks a variable speed dial, a chopper and a whisk. The black and red versions are the same machine.

Keep expectations in line. Blend soft foods, cut ingredients small and use short bursts. Do not use it with ice or hard frozen fruit, and do not submerge the motor body. If you find yourself wanting more power or finer control, the MasterChef or Cuisinart are the upgrade path.
products.bestFor: Occasional use in a small kitchen where low cost matters more than features.
pros: Low cost way to get a basic, working immersion blender
Pulse sensor allows short bursts for better control
Detachable shaft is dishwasher safe for easy cleaning
One year limited warranty plus US-based customer support
cons: Only 300W and two speeds, so power and control are basic
No whisk, chopper or beaker is included in the package
Not suited to ice, frozen fruit or hard vegetables

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 300 watt stick blends soup, sauces, baby food and soft smoothies, while a 400 watt model has more headroom for thicker mixes. The Cuisinart CSB-179 and OVENTE HS560B are 300 watts, and the Turelar and MasterChef are 400 watts. Watts measure input power, not blade performance, so a well-designed DC motor can outperform a higher-wattage cheap motor. Do not expect any of these to crush ice.

Variable speed lets you start slowly so hot liquid does not spray, then increase as the food breaks up. The Cuisinart and KitchenAid have continuous variable control, and the MasterChef has variable speed with a turbo button, while the Turelar, OVENTE and Bonsenkitchen have only two speeds. For soup and sauces, control matters more than top speed. A cheap two speed unit jumps from slow to fast and splashes.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Check the shaft length and diameter
buyingCriteria.explanation: An 8 inch shaft, as on the Cuisinart and KitchenAid, reaches the bottom of a quart jar or a deep pot. A slim shaft fits narrow jars and mason jars, but a shaft that is too short forces you to tilt the pot. Stainless steel shafts resist stains and odors better than plastic ones. Choose a shaft long enough for the deepest container you use.

A spinning blade can scratch nonstick and enamel pots. A blade guard, such as the Cuisinart bell and the KitchenAid removable pan guard, keeps the blade a small distance from the surface. A guard also reduces splatter by limiting how much liquid the blade can throw. If you cook in nonstick, put this near the top of your list.

Small motors overheat on long runs. The Bonsenkitchen listing says to run under 1 minute at a time and rest 30 minutes after 5 cycles. Most stick blenders are designed for short bursts. For batches that take several minutes, such as pureeing a large pot of soup, work in stages and let the motor cool.

A whisk and chopper, as in the Cuisinart kit, extend the tool but take storage space. A beaker or jar, as with the Bonsenkitchen and KitchenAid, simplifies small batches. In a small kitchen, a hanging ring, as on the Turelar, saves a drawer. Pick attachments you will use.

specDecoder.meaning: Watts measure the electrical power the motor draws. More watts allow thicker mixtures without stalling. The sticks here range from 300 to 400 watts.
specDecoder.watchFor: The KitchenAid and Bonsenkitchen listings give no wattage here. Treat power as unknown unless a listing states it.

specDecoder.meaning: A DC motor, as in the Cuisinart CSB-179, runs smoothly and quietly at variable speeds. Many budget sticks use a simpler AC universal motor that is louder.
specDecoder.watchFor: Listing wattage does not tell you the motor type. Look for a DC mention if quiet matters.

specDecoder.meaning: Continuous variable speed lets you set any speed between low and high, usually with a trigger or dial. Two speed models offer only low and high.
specDecoder.watchFor: A turbo button, as on the MasterChef and Turelar, is a boost, not a substitute for variable control.

specDecoder.meaning: The shaft is the stem that holds the blade. Eight inches reach deep pots and tall jars. A longer shaft needs a deeper container.
specDecoder.watchFor: Shaft length figures are sometimes measured including the blade bell. Check the usable depth.

specDecoder.meaning: Duty cycle is how long a motor can run before resting. Small blenders may allow one minute on and several minutes off. It protects the motor from heat.
specDecoder.watchFor: Few listings state duty cycle. The Bonsenkitchen is unusually honest about it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and control
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated wattage and speed control. The Cuisinart's DC motor and continuous speed and the KitchenAid's trigger led, the MasterChef followed with variable speed and turbo and the two speed models trailed.

howWeEvaluated.title: Shaft, blade and guard
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at shaft length, blade design and guards. The Cuisinart's 8 inch shaft and bell and the KitchenAid's pan guard rank highest for cookware protection, and the Turelar's two prong blade handles greens.

howWeEvaluated.title: Attachments and extras
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared included whisk, chopper, beaker and jar. The Cuisinart kit and the Bonsenkitchen 3-in-1 lead on extras, while the Turelar and OVENTE are bare sticks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted detachable shafts, dishwasher safe parts and hanging rings. All detach for cleaning, and the motor bodies are wiped only. The Turelar has a hanging ring.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value in the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed each blender by power and features. The OVENTE is the least expensive and simplest, and the Cuisinart and KitchenAid sit at the top. We favored machines that state honest limits.

howToChoose.intro: Match the tool to what you blend.

rows: Soup, sauces and herbs in small batches

howToChoose.intro: Control decides how messy the blending is.

cards.label: Variable speed
cards.text: The Cuisinart CSB-179, KitchenAid KHBV53 and MasterChef let you ramp speed smoothly. They suit hot soup and delicate emulsions, because you can start slow and avoid splashes.

cards.label: Two speed
cards.text: The Turelar, OVENTE and Bonsenkitchen offer low and high. They are simpler and cost less, but the jump between speeds is abrupt. They suit smoothies and thick sauces.

howToChoose.note: Pick variable speed if you blend hot liquids often. Pick two speed if you want a cheap tool for occasional use.

howToChoose.intro: Decide what extra jobs you want.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A small kitchen needs a slim shaft, a hook or ring for storage and a short list of attachments. Look for a detachable shaft that washes easily, and a motor that is not too large for a drawer.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Turelar has a hanging ring, and the Cuisinart kit packs a chopper and whisk. The Bonsenkitchen 3-in-1 gives a beaker for small batches.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you blend hot soup often or own nonstick pans. The Cuisinart CSB-179 and KitchenAid KHBV53 add variable control and cookware guards that save time and pans.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you blend once a week. The OVENTE HS560B or the Turelar handle light jobs, and extra features would go unused.

maintenance.why: Dried food clings to the blade and is hard to remove. Rinse in warm water or run the dishwasher if allowed.
The motor body must not be immersed. A damp cloth removes splashes.
A frayed cord is a shock risk. Replace the unit if damaged.
Small motors overheat on long runs. Rest after a minute of use.
A loose guard can touch the blade. Reseat or replace it.
Moisture causes odor and corrosion. Hang or store with the shaft dry.

faq.q: Is 300 watts enough for an immersion blender?
faq.a: Yes for soup, sauces, baby food and soft smoothies. A 300 watt model such as the Cuisinart CSB-179 handles these well. It is not suited to ice or heavy frozen fruit.

faq.q: Can I use an immersion blender in a nonstick pot?
faq.a: Yes with a guard. The KitchenAid pan guard and the Cuisinart bell keep the blade away from the surface. Without a guard, tilt the blade and avoid scraping the pot.
Splashing comes from starting at high speed or lifting the blade out of the liquid. Start slow, keep the blade submerged and use a tall container. A guard also reduces splatter.

faq.q: How long can I run an immersion blender?
faq.a: Short runs of about a minute are typical for small motors. The Bonsenkitchen listing says to rest 30 minutes after five cycles. For large batches, work in stages.

faq.q: Can I wash the whole blender?
faq.a: No. The shaft detaches and can be washed or put in the dishwasher where allowed, but the motor body must only be wiped. Never immerse it.

faq.q: Is a hand blender better than a countertop blender?
faq.a: For soup in the pot and small batches, yes. It is easier to clean and store. For ice, frozen fruit and large smoothies, a countertop blender is stronger.
